newsitem.title: FRANCE: Credit Lyonnais board reviews recovery plan.
newsitem.headline: Credit Lyonnais board reviews recovery plan.

text.p: The board of Credit Lyonnais met on Thursday to discuss the troubled bank's privatisation stragegy but bank officials said there was still no decision on how much state aid the bank will need to find a buyer.

That figure is the focus of intense negotiations between the state-controlled bank and the finance ministry, people close to the talks said. The sum most persistently mentioned in press reports is 12 billion francs ($2.26 billion).
Credit Lyonnais chairman Jean Peyrelevade named that amount last year as the figure needed to boost the bank's solvency ratios to levels to allow it to be sold under the best terms.
The bank, which limped back to profit last year, still is struggling to put behind it the legacy of an acquisition binge in the late 1980s that brought it to the brink of collapse.
Bank officials said the board meeting was intended to give members a chance to examine the plan, already submitted to the centre-right government, and declined further commment.
The government has helped out the bank three times, pumping in billions of francs and underwriting a so-called "bad bank" in 1995 to hold its shaky assets.
It says it wants a fast privatisation and has pledged to inject more money to ready it for sale but "the (sell-off) plan still has to be completed," a government official said.
The European Commission must approve any fresh state aid.
If the 12 billion franc figure is right, the state will have injected more than 20 billion francs into Credit Lyonnais's balance sheet since 1994.

On top of that cost, business weekly L'Expansion said estimated losses on sales of assets shifted from the bank into the separate entity known as the Consortium de Realisation (CDR) would hit 90 billion francs.

Added to that figure would be carrying costs of 30 billion francs, it said. However, the final loss total will not be known until completion of the asset sale programme, set for 2014. ($1=5.307 French Franc)
